ety.text: From Middle English left, luft, leoft, lift, lyft, from Old English left, lyft (“weak, clumsy, foolish”), attested in Old English lyftādl (“palsy, paralysis”), from Proto-Germanic *luft-, from *lubjaną (“to castrate, lop off”) (compare dialectal English lib, West Frisian lobje, Dutch lubben), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)lewp-, *(s)lup- (“hanging limply”). Compare Scots left (“left”), North Frisian lefts, leeft, leefts (“left”), West Frisian lofts (“left”), obsolete Dutch lucht, leftsch, lefts, lefs (“left”), dialectal Dutch loof (“weak, worthless”), archaic Low German lucht (“left”).
From Middle English left, variant of laft (“remaining, left”), from Old English lǣfed, ġelǣfed, past participle of lǣfan (“to leave”). More at leave.

senses.d: Designating the side of the body toward the west when one is facing north; the side of the body on which the heart is located in most humans; the opposite of right. This arrow points to the reader's left: ←
Anticlockwise, particularly when describing a change in direction or orientation.
ex: The road up ahead contains a left bend.
Rotate the bolt to the left to loosen it.

senses.d: Designating the bank of a river (etc.) on one's left when facing downstream (i.e. facing forward while floating with the current); that is, the north bank of a river that flows eastward. If this arrow: ⥲ shows the direction of the current, the tilde is on the left side of the river.
ex: The Eiffel Tower is on the left bank of the Seine.

senses.d: Left-wing; pertaining to the political left.
Relating to the beginning or earlier part of a phrase.

ex: Turn left at the corner. NO! Your other left.
The East Coast of the US leans left in elections.

senses.d: The left-wing political parties as a group; citizens holding left-wing views as a group.
ex: The Left left workers behind, thinking they had a winning demographic coalition. It hasn't really worked out for them yet.

senses.d: A punch delivered with the left fist.
ex: The world 'as got me snouted jist a treat; Crool Forchin's dirty left 'as smote me soul.

senses.d: A wave breaking from left to right (viewed from the shore).

ety.text: From gauchir (“to bend, dodge, warp”), a conflation of Old French gauchier (“to tread”) (from Frankish *walkijan, *walkan, cognate with English walk) + Old French guenchir (“to deviate”) (from Frankish *wenkijan (“to sway, falter”)).
Learned borrowing from Latin sinister. Doublet of sinestro.
Borrowed from Basque ezkerra, absolutive singular form of ezker (“left”). Cognate with Catalan esquerra and Portuguese esquerda. Displaced siniestra.

ety.text: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese esquerdo, from Old Spanish exquerdo, from Basque ezkerra, absolutive of ezker (“left hand; left side”), from Proto-Basque *ezkeR (“left hand”). Cognate with Asturian izquierdu, Catalan esquerre, Galician esquerdo, xiquerdo, Ladino izkierdo, Leonese esquierdu, Spanish izquierdo.
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese sẽestro, from Late Latin sinextrum. Compare Spanish siniestro. Doublet of sinistro.
